source_text: it seems like it would be unfortunate if we had to recheck all compiled matching rows cold each time we fixed something.  hopefully the audit is fast, e.g., based on function calls rather than behaviour?

fragments.text: it seems like it would be unfortunate if we had to recheck all compiled matching rows cold each time we fixed something.
e.g., based on function calls rather than behaviour?

reply_text:
㊥ The audit already compares terms, not behaviour. Its cost is the cold compile: before the port can show its terms for a row, it has to compile everything that row depends on, starting from an empty cache. That took 5 to 20 minutes per row, so 20 rows across 4 lanes took about 75 minutes. Rechecking all correct rows after every fix would cost that each time. Your suggestion to go by function calls would cut most of it: record which parts of the port's compiler each row goes through, and recheck only the rows a fix touches.

🈖 ("based on function calls rather than behaviour") Each audit lane runs the comparator: it captures the port's elaborated terms and compares them node by node with Lean's dump. No `#eval` behaviour checks run, and the comparison itself takes seconds. The time goes on the compile before it. The port compiles from source, so even `Lean.Syntax.isNone` first compiles parts of `Init`, `Array` and `Syntax`. Of the 20 lanes, 19 finished between 09:39 and 10:54.

㊭ (cheaper rechecks) Two changes, in this order:
1. **Recheck only the rows a fix can affect.** On one cold run, record which functions in the port's compiler each correct row goes through (Python's tracer, once per row). When a fix changes some of those functions, recheck only the rows that went through them. Most fixes touch one elaborator path, such as structure instances or do-notation lifting, so most rows would be skipped. A safe default for a fix to shared code is to recheck everything. We'd also need a check that the recorded function list is complete. A planted change to a function must flag its rows.
2. **Run one cold compile for all rows together.** The rows share most of their dependencies, so one fresh compile in one process can capture terms for every correct row. That's still cold for deciding a merge, and it costs about one large compile instead of twenty. We first chose one cache per row so that rows couldn't contaminate each other through the cache. Within one fresh run, that worry doesn't apply.

🈝 (the warm cache) The proper fix is a warm cache we can trust: one that includes the compiler's own version in its key. Then a recheck would recompile only what the fix changed. We haven't found the cause of the warm-vs-cold difference yet, so cold stays the rule for decisions until we do.

㊯ (next) When codex-23 finishes lane 807 and writes `AUDIT-20.md`, I'll give it change 1 as a small packet, since it wrote the capture tool. Change 2 follows if change 1 holds up.

previous_reply_acts.text: ("the only thing that can be trusted ... is this comparator") Agreed: no more questions for you. The loop is: run the rows; on an error, use the comparator, cold; fix the port until it matches Lean. I've written that into the park reminder and into my saved memory.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text: ("code that you said was compliant with Lean") You're right to question it. The 20 rows in Rob's main were accepted because their behaviour matched native Lean on preregistered inputs and their instance choices matched. Most of them were never compared with Lean term by term, and the comparator didn't exist when they were accepted. So "compliant" meant "behaves the same on the tested inputs", which is weaker than what you're asking for now.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-4
previous_reply_acts.text:
(comparator work) I've sent codex-23 two jobs (`invoke-…32776`):
1. **Make the comparator properly cold.** Add a `--cold` option that deletes the whole compiled cache before capturing, because warm captures gave different results this morning.
2. **Audit the 20 accepted rows with it.** Dump Lean's terms where they're missing, capture each row cold in its own worktree, and compare. The results go to `AUDIT-20.md`, listing per row how many nodes match, differ or weren't produced, and the first real difference. Any row with a real difference goes back into the fix loop, including what's already in Rob's main.
